prompt.context: Your client, Big Island Surfboards, is a surfboard manufacturer based in Hawaii. The CEO wants to expand the company's product line and revenues and is thinking of entering the market for surfboard wax. It hired you to calculate the market size for wax, and your firm determined that the market size for surfboard wax is about $6M a year with about 3 million bars sold annually. Your firm also found that the market was fairly competitive with three large global players all based outside of Hawaii controlling about 70% of the market, and smaller niche companies including a few based in Hawaii accounting for the remaining 30%. The client was impressed with our work and believes that its unique brand and connection to Hawaii will enable it to succeed in capturing a piece of the pie. It wants to move forward with entering the market.
prompt.question: The client has now asked us to determine how they should enter the market for surfboard wax. How would you think about this problem?

clarifying_info.a: Surfboard wax comes in a bar form (similar to soap) and is used to coat the top of the surfboard in order to provide surfers with a surface that their feet can grip.

framework: Market entry options: (1) Build capability organically — invest in R&D and manufacturing; (2) Acquire a wax manufacturer; (3) Joint venture with an existing manufacturer; (4) Contract out production and resell under client brand; (5) License Big Island Surfboards brand to another wax company

Profitability tree — Revenue side: Price × Quantity. Average market price = $6M / 3M bars = $2/bar (brand premium could justify $3). Quantity depends on strategy and achievable market share (reasonable range 5–15%, i.e. 150k–450k bars)

Profitability tree — Cost side: Variable costs (raw wax/scent materials, packaging, shipping); Fixed costs (rent, labor, SG&A, marketing). For contract arrangement, variable costs are absorbed by contractor (charged as a per-unit price to client)

Qualitative pros/cons for each option: Option 1 — highest potential return but requires significant R&D/capex investment; Option 2 — costly and logistically complex but provides established product line and distribution; Option 3 — spreads cost/risk but ties client to a potentially complicated partner; Option 4 — enables quick production but creates dependency on contractor's capacity and willingness; Option 5 — steady revenue stream but surrenders brand control

questions.prompt: After reviewing qualitative pros/cons, the client rules out organic growth and joint venture (too complex/risky) and rules out licensing (wants brand control). It narrows to Acquisition or Contracting. For the Acquisition option: Aloha Surf Wax sells bars at $2.50 to retailers, has COGS of $0.50/bar, annual fixed costs of $300k, holds 10% of the total market in Hawaii, and the owner wants $1M. Calculate whether the acquisition earns a return within 5 years (no discounting).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a simple P&L: Revenue = 10% × 3M bars × $2.50 = $750k; COGS = 10% × 3M × $0.50 = $150k; SG&A = $300k; Annual Profit = $750k − $150k − $300k = $300k. Over 5 years: $300k × 5 = $1.5M. Net of purchase price: $1.5M − $1M = $500k positive return. Acquisition earns a return within 5 years.

math.setup: Annual Revenue = market share × total bars × price per bar; Annual Profit = Revenue − COGS − Fixed Costs; 5-year return = Annual Profit × 5 − acquisition price

questions.prompt: For the Contracting option: Maui Surf Wax will produce 300k bars/year at $1.50/bar to our client. Client projects selling all inventory to retailers at $3.00/bar. Maui charges a one-time $100k reconfiguration fee. Annual fixed costs (marketing, sales, SG&A) are $300k. Calculate whether contracting earns a return within 5 years (no discounting).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a simple P&L: Revenue = 300k × $3.00 = $900k; COGS = 300k × $1.50 = $450k; SG&A = $300k; Annual Profit = $900k − $450k − $300k = $150k. Over 5 years: $150k × 5 = $750k. Net of one-time fee: $750k − $100k = $650k. Contracting earns a return within 5 years and yields more net cash than acquisition.

math.setup: Annual Revenue = bars × selling price; Annual Profit = Revenue − COGS − Fixed Costs; 5-year return = Annual Profit × 5 − one-time setup fee

recommendation: Recommend Big Island Surfboards enter the surfboard wax market by contracting production to Maui Surf Wax and reselling under the Big Island Surfboards brand
Contracting yields a $650k net return on a $100k initial investment over 5 years, versus $500k net return on a $1M acquisition investment — contracting is both higher-returning and capital-efficient
Contracting enables faster market entry, lower upfront capital at risk, and leverages Big Island's brand strength without a costly acquisition
risks: Maui Surf Wax may reduce excess capacity allocated to Big Island production in the future
Quality control issues in production are outside Big Island's direct control
Dependency on a single contractor creates supply concentration risk
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on other potential acquisition or contracting targets to see if better deal terms are available
Revisit options initially ruled out (organic growth, joint venture) if contracting arrangement proves unsatisfactory
Negotiate contractual protections (minimum capacity commitments, quality standards, IP ownership) with Maui Surf Wax
